opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about it less as a threat and more as validation. When you see organizations with the resources and talent of Boston Dynamics or Google DeepMind putting serious effort into humanoids and embodied AI, it tells customers and investors that this isn't science fiction. It's a real category, and it's coming. That rising tide helps everyone building in the space.

That said, I don't want to be naive about it. These are formidable teams. Boston Dynamics has decades of experience in dynamic locomotion and mechanical design, and what they've done with balance and mobility is remarkable. DeepMind brings some of the deepest expertise in the world in learning systems, reinforcement learning, and large-scale models, and they're clearly pushing hard on robot foundation models.

Where I think we compete is focus. We've made a deliberate bet that the hardest and most valuable problem in general-purpose robotics isn't walking or doing backflips. It's the hands and the mind behind them: dexterous manipulation and the intelligence to do useful work in messy, real-world environments. Most of the economic value of human labor is in what we do with our hands. If you can't reliably grasp, manipulate, and use tools the way people do, you don't really have a general-purpose robot, no matter how well it moves.

Second, we've been very customer-driven. We've been putting systems into real commercial settings, learning what breaks, and feeding that back into the hardware and the AI. That deployment loop generates data and insight you can't get in a lab, and it compounds over time.

Third, this market is going to be enormous. There are tens of millions of unfilled jobs and labor shortages across logistics, manufacturing, retail, and elsewhere. This isn't a winner-take-all situation in the near term. There will be room for multiple successful companies, likely specializing in different capabilities or verticals.

So yes, we watch the big players closely and respect them a lot. But I'd rather be a focused company with a clear thesis, moving quickly with customers, than try to out-spend anyone. Speed, focus, and real-world learning are how a company our size wins.

r003.rationale: It calls Boston Dynamics formidable but does not compare the companies’ progress relative to their time in robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think of it as a threat so much as validation. When Boston Dynamics or DeepMind puts serious resources into humanoids, it tells everyone, investors, customers, talent, that this category is real. A few years ago I spent half my time convincing people humanoids weren't science fiction. I don't have to do that anymore, and frankly those companies did a lot of that work for me.

Where it gets interesting is what each of us is actually good at. Boston Dynamics has the best hardware pedigree in the world, no question. Atlas is a marvel. But a marvel in a lab and a product on a factory floor are different things, and their history is more research than deployment at scale. DeepMind is coming at it from the other direction. They have extraordinary models and the compute to train them, but a robot foundation model is only as good as the body it's running on and the data you can collect from real environments. Neither of those is a software problem.

Our bet has always been the boring middle. Build a platform that's cheap enough and reliable enough that a customer will actually put twenty of them in a warehouse, then use those deployments to generate the data that makes the next version better. That flywheel is hard to copy, because it requires being in the field, dealing with dropped totes and bad lighting and a supervisor who's annoyed the robot blocked a forklift. You don't learn that in simulation.

So the honest answer is the threat I worry about isn't either of those names. It's whoever figures out the manufacturing cost curve first. If someone can build a capable humanoid for a fraction of what it costs today, that resets the whole game. That's where I keep my attention.

astra-6.text:
I take them seriously. But I think the key question is: what problem are you solving for the customer? A robot can be impressive in a demonstration, but putting it to work means making it reliable, safe, and economical, day after day.

So I don’t see this as a race where whoever has the most impressive humanoid automatically wins. There are a lot of different jobs to do, and there’s room for different approaches. Our focus has to be on delivering something customers can actually use and justify paying for. Those companies create competitive pressure, certainly, but advances in the underlying technology can also help move the whole industry forward.

sol-6.1.text:
I take them seriously. But I think the real question is: can you put a robot into a customer’s operation and have it do useful work reliably, at a cost that makes sense? That’s a different challenge from showing an impressive capability in a controlled environment.

Boston Dynamics and Google DeepMind bring significant capabilities to this space. We have to stay focused on the customer problem—what task needs to get done, what happens when something goes wrong, and how much support the robot needs. There’s room for multiple companies here, but ultimately we’ll be judged by how well our robots perform in the field.

r001.rationale: It contrasts controlled demonstrations with useful, reliable work in a customer operation, but does not identify Boston Dynamics’ replica factory site or distinguish it from an operating manufacturing line.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether a task solves a customer problem, but does not mention Boston Dynamics’ rack-to-table transfers or explain how those differ from an actual manufacturing need.

r003.rationale: It says the companies have significant capabilities and that LeBlanc takes them seriously; it does not compare their progress in robotics relative to how long they have been in the field.
